newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia party says no formal opposition alliance.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia party says no formal opposition alliance.

text.p: Indonesia's Moslem-based minority party said no formal alliance had been agreed with the ousted leader of a rival party ahead of this month's general election, the Antara news agency reported on Saturday.

The state news agency quoted Tosari Widjaja, secretary-general of the United Development Party (PPP), as saying his grouping had no formal understanding with ousted leader of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) Megawati Sukarnoputri.
The PPP sent its branch leader in Solo, Central Java, to meet Megawati, daughter of Indonesia's late founding president Sukarno, on Tuesday in an attempt to woo her and her supporters.
Megawati has not made any comment but sources close to her said a decision on how to respond to the PPP's advances would be taken soon.
Scores of Megawati's supporters were seen at PPP rallies in a number of cities in Java, including the capital Jakarta, in the past week, suggesting an alliance was taking shape.

The Christian-Nationalist PDI split into two camps after Megawati was ousted by a government-backed faction last year. The government does not recognise Megawati's faction and has barred it from contesting the May 29 elections.

The PPP and the government-backed PDI faction are battling the much-larger ruling Golkar party in the elections, at which Golkar is seeking to push its share of the vote to more than 70 percent from the 68 percent it won at the last polls in 1992. The PPP won 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent.
The Jakarta Post newspaper quoted a study by the independent Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) as saying that Indonesia's election system was flawed and designed to favour Golkar.

The newspaper quoted the report as saying that all the laws and state institutions relating to the election were in the ruling party's favour. It said the laws also allowed manipulation and poll rigging.
"It is not surprising, therefore, that many people consider the general election as a mere formality and a waste of money," said the CSIS, which groups political scientists and economists.

The split in the PDI would buttress the already overwhelming superiority of Golkar, it said, adding that the ruling party would increase its absolute majority in parliament and the PPP would gain more seats at the cost of the PDI.
